Title: [Excerpt from] “Brrr: Growing Up in Antarctica”
Author: by Jodi Forschmiedt
Content: A baby emperor penguin escapes the warm embrace of his parent. Squawking loudly, the featherless infant thrashes about on the ice. His mother quickly scoops the chick back to the safety of her brood pouch, a flap of blubbery skin hanging down from her belly...

Every other bird in Antarctica migrates, traveling `text(north)` to warmer climates when `text(winter)` comes. But the hardy emperor penguins stay, and their chicks hatch in the coldest place on `text(Earth)`. The temperatures usually fall to around `text(40 degrees)` below `text(zero)`! To withstand the subfreezing temperatures and protect their chicks, emperor penguins use a combination of teamwork and unique characteristics.

The `text(first)` challenge an emperor faces is just being born! Female penguins each lay `text(one)` softball-sized egg and then head out to sea to hunt and feed on krill, squid, and fish. Caring for the egg is Dad's job. The male emperor keeps the egg warm by holding it on top of his feet. His brood pouch hangs down over the egg, insulating it from the frigid air...

Male emperors hold the eggs for over `text(two months)`. During that time, they can't eat or even move very much. Penguin dads weigh around `text(70 pounds)`, about as much as an average `text(ten-year-old)` kid. But while baby-sitting their eggs, they can lose up to `text(half)` their weight!

Emperor dads are well-equipped for their long fast. Over the `text(summer)`, they stuff themselves with squid and fish to build up plenty of fat on their bodies in order to survive without eating for `text(months)`. In fact, fat is the reason only male emperor penguins can tackle the job of caring for the eggs. Females are smaller and can't build up enough fat to survive the fast.

A penguin standing alone on the ice wouldn't live through the `text(winter)`. He would use up his store of body fat too quickly. But the emperors help each other: all the dads in the colony huddle together with their backs to the wind to increase warmth and save their energy.

The whole time Dad's caring for the egg, Mom's at sea. Since the other seabirds have migrated `text(north)`, the emperors get all the food to themselves. So Mom eats enough to fatten up and store additional food in her stomach. When she returns to the colony around the time the chick hatches, Mom coughs up the stored food and feeds it to her chick. When Mom takes over care of the newly hatched little `text(one)`, Dad gratefully leaves to find his first meal in `text(months)`. He'll soon return with more food for the chick. Raising a baby is hard work!

Emperor chicks have to stay snuggled in their parents' brood pouches, because they start life naked. Adult emperors definitely aren't naked — they keep out the cold with layers of “clothes.” An undercoat of soft, downy feathers traps their body heat. Long, stiff, overlapping feathers keep out the wind. An oily substance the penguins make in their glands coats the feathers, making them waterproof. And, of course, that thick layer of fat insulates their bodies.

Emperor parents protect their young until the chicks have grown feathers, when they're around `text(seven weeks)` old. Then it's time for more teamwork. The chicks of the colony huddle together in groups called crèches. A crèche is like a penguin day-care center! While their parents hunt, the chicks keep each other warm. The adults return when they can to feed their chicks. They know their babies are safe — Antarctica is so cold and barren in the `text(winter)` that no hungry land predators live there...

When emperors reach their `text(fourth year)`, they are all grown up ... The penguin who `text(once)` tried to escape his mother's brood pouch now uses his own to keep an egg warm and safe from the cold Antarctic `text(winter)`.
